## Conclusion

Yes, conditionally: the record assembled here supports adopting a targeted voucher program with fiscal guardrails and enough participating-school capacity, but it does not support a promise that every participant's test scores will rise. A broad research synthesis reports mixed participant test-score results alongside more favourable findings on attainment and parent satisfaction [1]. A national fiscal model estimates savings across many existing programs, but those estimates depend on how many recipients would otherwise attend public school and on which district costs can adjust [2]. The strongest opposing view is that vouchers drain district resources while offering too few usable alternatives. The evidence reviewed below answers the first concern only conditionally and confirms that the second can bind [2][5].

## Key findings

- A 2025 synthesis organizes more than 200 studies by participant achievement and attainment, parent satisfaction, public-school effects, fiscal effects and four other outcomes [1].
- Its participant test-score evidence is mixed rather than a uniform positive result, so the case cannot rest on achievement alone [1].
- A fiscal analysis covers 40 private-choice programs in 19 states and Washington, D.C., using lower- and upper-bound cost assumptions rather than one universal saving [2].
- An Indiana study finds little average effect, positive or negative, on students remaining in public schools, with small positive effects for low-income students [3].
- A national capacity study reports that the limited programs it examined had not increased private-school enrollment or capacity, a constraint on how many families could use a voucher [5].

## The strongest counterargument

The objection with the most political weight is that a voucher program is a transfer out of the district system: a departing student can take funding immediately while buildings, transport and staffing do not shrink at the same speed. Families also cannot exercise a nominal choice if no suitable private school has space nearby. Stated at full strength, the claim is that the program can weaken the schools most children remain in while directing public money to an option many families cannot actually use.

The record gives a limited answer, not a dismissal. The fiscal model separates short-run variable costs from long-run total costs and makes the number of students switching out of public school an explicit assumption [2]. The Indiana analysis finds little average academic effect on public-school students rather than the broad harm the objection predicts, while finding small gains for low-income students [3]. But the capacity study reports no general expansion of private-school enrollment or supply under the programs it examined [5]. Adoption therefore depends on a state-specific fiscal estimate, gradual funding changes and evidence that usable seats exist; without those, the objection would overturn the recommendation.

## Evidence on participant outcomes

The 2025 *123s of School Choice* is a synthesis rather than a new experiment. It groups more than 200 empirical studies into eight outcome areas, including participant test scores, educational attainment and parent satisfaction [1]. Its summarized test-score record contains positive, null and negative findings, while the attainment and satisfaction sections are more favourable. That pattern supports treating outcomes separately rather than converting them into one claim that vouchers "work."

The parent evidence answers a different question again. A survey of families using Georgia's tax-credit scholarship program examines why parents selected private schools and what they valued in them [4]. It can describe participant preferences and satisfaction, but a voluntary parent survey cannot by itself establish achievement effects or represent families who applied and did not participate.

The appropriate conclusion is therefore narrower than a single effect size: the assembled record provides reasons families value access and evidence of favourable outcomes in parts of the literature, while also recording mixed achievement results [1][4]. A state should define in advance whether it is trying to improve test scores, attainment, family fit or some combination, because those outcomes are not interchangeable.

## Fiscal impact

Lueken's national analysis compares the public cost of 40 choice programs with estimated savings when participants switch from public schools [2]. Its short-run bound counts costs that can adjust with enrollment; its long-run bound allows a broader set of costs, including facilities, to adjust. The result is a range, not a fixed saving that can be transferred unchanged to a new state.

The switcher rate is load-bearing. A voucher used by a child who would otherwise remain in private school adds public cost without reducing public-school enrollment, while a public-school student who switches creates some offset [2]. Program price, district funding rules and the timing of staffing changes must therefore enter the state estimate before adoption.

## Effects on public schools and program design

Egalite and Catt's Indiana analysis uses distance to participating private schools to estimate effects on students remaining in traditional public schools. It finds little evidence of an average positive or negative effect, with consistent small positive effects for low-income students [3]. That result rejects both a blanket harm claim and a blanket competition-gain claim.

Supply is a separate constraint. Carpenter, Keith and Catt report that the programs and period they studied had not produced increased private-school enrollment or capacity, although they also did not find the increase in racial segregation critics predicted [5]. A state should therefore pair eligibility with verified seat availability, phase funding so district costs can adjust, and publish participant and non-participant outcomes. Those conditions are part of the recommendation, not implementation details.
